steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Every five minutes—the span of 300 seconds—Elias would turn the great brass wheel, sending the Fresnel lens spinning once more. In the dim lantern room of Seabright Point, the rotation brought a steady pulse of light across the black waves below. Storm clouds curled on the horizon, and each flash was a promise to any mariner out there: “You are seen. You are guided.”

That evening, the wind carried an unfamiliar urgency. Elias pressed his forehead against the cold window, counting the seconds between each beam, as he always did. His father, the keeper before him, had taught him that in those intervals lay both duty and hope: duty to keep vigil, hope that a single blink might save a life.

A distant horn answered the beacon. Rain pelted the windows in heavy sheets, and the sea roared against the cliffs. Elias paused only to check the oil reservoir and tighten a loose gear. Then, hand on the wheel again, he felt the old rhythm settle into his bones—tick, spin, flash; tick, spin, flash. Time was measured here not by hours or days, but by the lamp’s steady arc.

Suddenly, through the storm-sheared darkness, Elias saw her: the shattered hulk of a fishing boat, stranded on hidden shoals. With no time to lose, he lit the signal cannon, sending a flare skyward. Moments later, a rescue launch answered the call, navigating safely toward shore by the lighthouse’s unwavering glow.

When dawn broke, the storm spent its fury, and the sea lay calm. Elias stood once more beside the wheel, exhaustion and relief interwoven in his chest. In those silent 300-second intervals, he had kept his promise—to be the steadfast eye of safety for everyone lost at sea. And for him, that was no small measure of time at all.
